Object-oriented programming, or OOP, is a paradigm that organizes code around objects, which are entities that bundle data and behavior together. OOP emphasizes modularity, reusability, and extensibility through encapsulation, which hides internals, inheritance, which enables code reuse through hierarchies, and polymorphism, where objects respond differently to the same message. While OOP is powerful for large systems, it has trade-offs in complexity and sometimes enforces structures that don't fit all problems naturally.

The four pillars of OOP are essential. Encapsulation bundles data and methods in a class and uses access modifiers like public and private to control what's visible. Abstraction hides implementation details and exposes only necessary interfaces. Inheritance lets you derive new classes from existing ones to reuse and extend behavior. Polymorphism lets objects of different types respond to the same method call in different ways through method overriding and interfaces.

Core concepts matter deeply. A class is a template that defines an object's structure and behavior. Instances are the actual objects created from that template. Instance variables hold the data associated with an object, its state. Methods are functions associated with an object that operate on its state. Constructors are special methods that initialize an object when it's created. Static members are data or methods shared by all instances of a class, belonging to the class itself rather than to individual instances.

Inheritance and hierarchies are how OOP achieves code reuse. Some languages like Java, C++, and Python support single inheritance, where a class inherits from one parent. Others like C++ and Python allow multiple inheritance, where a class inherits from multiple parents. This can cause ambiguity, known as the diamond problem. Interfaces are contracts that specify methods without providing implementation. A class implements an interface. Abstract classes provide partial implementation and cannot be instantiated directly, only inherited from.

Good OOP design follows certain principles. DRY—Don't Repeat Yourself—means write code once and reuse it through inheritance or composition. SOLID is an acronym for five principles: Single Responsibility, Open and Closed, Liskov Substitution, Interface Segregation, and Dependency Inversion. Sometimes composition, using objects as components, is cleaner than deep inheritance hierarchies.

Common pitfalls trip up many programmers. Tight coupling means objects depend heavily on each other, so refactoring in one place breaks code everywhere. Deep inheritance hierarchies are hard to understand and maintain. It's usually better to keep trees shallow or use composition. Violating the Liskov Substitution Principle means a subclass doesn't properly replace its parent, which breaks polymorphism.

Object-oriented programming dominated software engineering for over thirty years and remains the paradigm of choice for large systems developed by teams. Operating systems, game engines, and enterprise applications all rely on OOP. Its strength lies in modularity and the intuitive mapping between code and real-world entities like users, accounts, and transactions. But OOP is not universal. Functional programming is gaining favor for concurrent and distributed systems where immutability and pure functions offer clarity. Modern languages increasingly blend paradigms. Python supports OOP but encourages functional techniques. Rust uses OOP-like traits alongside functional patterns. The real skill is knowing when OOP is the right fit and when its complexity becomes more burden than benefit. It connects closely to type systems, which rely on class hierarchies and type checking. And algorithm choice is independent of paradigm, though OOP structures how algorithms are actually implemented.
